As entropy decreases in human health systems due to medical progress, disease prevalence diminishes. This is modeled through exponential decay functions where pathogen load P(t) decreases over time t, governed by therapeutic efficacy. Surgical advancement S(t) enhances the system's ability to intervene at critical points, increasing survival probability. The interplay between these variables creates a dynamic equilibrium where entropy reduction leads to improved societal resilience against disease. Failure modes arise when entropy begins to rise again due to antibiotic resistance or lack of public health infrastructure, indicating a breakdown in the system's ability to maintain low pathogen loads.
